Why local-first software is quietly winning

In 2025, a survey of 2,400 developers found that 61% said offline capability was a deciding factor when choosing a productivity tool. The study was conducted by the Local Software Alliance and published in the Journal of Applied Systems.

The shift away from the cloud

Several popular note-taking apps now sync locally first and upload later. The architecture reverses the traditional client-server assumption: the source of truth lives on the device, and the cloud is a mirror, not the master.

One developer reported that switching to a local-first tool cut their sync-related bugs by 74%. Their team measured the drop over a six-month period after migrating two internal services.

What this means for users

Local-first tools tend to feel faster because reads never wait on a network round-trip. For a 10MB note database, first-frame load measured 40ms locally versus 900ms when served from a remote API.

Privacy is the other headline benefit: content that never leaves the device cannot be leaked in a server breach. In 2024, at least 12 documented breaches exposed cloud-synced user data, while local-first systems reported none from server-side storage.

It remains unclear whether local-first will dominate large collaborative projects, where multi-user conflict resolution is still an open problem. Some teams report that merge conflicts appear more often than with live multiplayer sync.

Considerations and trade-offs

Critics argue local-first apps make it harder to build shareable workflows and that backups become the user's responsibility. "If your laptop dies and you never synced, the data is gone," one engineer warned.

Maybe the trend will peak, perhaps it will plateau, but adoption numbers continue to climb each quarter according to the Alliance's tracker.

For teams that value speed and privacy, trying a local-first tool is a low-risk experiment: install it, run the same workflow for two weeks, and compare time-to-task against the previous stack.
